title: Oscar and the House
premise: Jonah Okonkwo, a nonbinary urban explorer, returns to their decaying hometown after their grandmother's death and finds 'Oscar'—the imaginary friend they buried in memory at age seven—waiting on the porch, unchanged for thirty years. Oscar is not imaginary but a tenant of the House, a structure that exists beneath and behind the town, feeding on what its residents surrender: names, years, children. In 1974 Jonah's grandmother took something from the House—a ledger of debts owed—and the family has paid interest ever since, which is why Jonah's father vanished and why Jonah's childhood was haunted. To end it, Jonah must descend through the unmapped tunnels with Oscar as an increasingly unreliable guide, return the ledger, and decide whether 'returning' includes themselves. In the end Jonah pays the debt not with their life but with their belonging to the surface world, becoming the House's new archivist—freeing Oscar, saving the town, and losing the ordinary life they were only beginning to want.
about_author: Edmund Hartwell is the pen name of a former surveyor who spent a decade mapping municipal infrastructure in the Rust Belt and swears three of his tunnels were never approved by anyone. He writes horror from a house he refuses to describe in detail.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Returning to Hollow Creek for their grandmother's funeral, Jonah finds a small figure on the porch steps—Oscar, exactly as remembered at age seven, unaged, unblinking. The emotional beat is dread braided with shameful nostalgia; the reader feels the pull of something loved that should be feared.

chapters.title: Inventory of the Dead
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Clearing the grandmother's house, Jonah finds a locked tin under the floorboards containing a child's drawing of a door and a note: 'It's not a debt if you never open it.' Neighbors watch from yards, silent. Beat: grief curdling into suspicion.

chapters.title: What Oscar Said in 1974
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, seven-year-old Jonah's POV. The summer of the father's disappearance: Oscar's games, the humming in the walls, the night mother burned the drawings and told Jonah never to say the name again. Beat: the reader assembles what the child could not.

chapters.title: The Survey That Doesn't Exist
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, professional mode. Consulting old municipal maps, Jonah discovers the tunnels they explored for twelve years appear on no record—except one 1973 survey sheet, stamped VOID, signed by their grandmother. Beat: the explorer's competence becomes a trap.

chapters.title: Oscar Explains the Rules
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Oscar appears inside the locked house and lays out the terms: the House holds the ledger; the ledger was taken in 1974; interest accrues in people. He is gentle, patient, and wrong about something he refuses to name. Beat: seductive clarity.

chapters.title: Debts of the Living
chapters.summary: POV of Ruth, a neighbor. Ruth reveals that half the town's families 'owe'—her own son went into the tunnels at nineteen and came back with someone else's memories. She warns Jonah that the House lets you in free and charges for the exit. Beat: communal horror.

chapters.title: The First Door
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Following the VOID survey's route, Jonah finds a door in a storm tunnel that opens onto the grandmother's kitchen—1974, dust-free, mid-afternoon forever. They take the ledger from the table and the kitchen begins to scream. Beat: transgression and immediate consequence.

chapters.title: Interest
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Above ground, hours have become days; Jonah's reflection lags, then smiles without them. Oscar appears distressed—genuinely, Jonah thinks—and urges them deeper before the House 'adjusts the account.' Beat: body horror as bookkeeping.

chapters.title: The Archivist Below
chapters.summary: POV of the Archivist, in second person. A brief, chilling interlude: the entity that keeps the ledger describes its work—recording surrenders, cataloguing the town's quiet trades—and notes a discrepancy from 1974 it has waited fifty years to correct. Beat: the antagonist's cold perspective.

chapters.title: Mother's Confession
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. A phone call with the estranged mother, who finally admits she helped grandmother steal the ledger to buy back Jonah's father—and that it bought back the wrong person, or something wearing him. Beat: family as complicity; inheritance as curse.

chapters.title: Down the Unmapped Way
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, with Oscar. The descent proper: tunnels that rearrange behind them, rooms furnished from Jonah's childhood, a staircase of doors each labeled with a family name. Oscar grows strange near the House's heart. Beat: wonder curdling into claustrophobia.

chapters.title: The Room of Jonah
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. They find a room containing every version of themselves the House has kept—child, teenager, the adult who never left. One of the Jonans speaks: the House doesn't collect people, it grows them. Beat: identity horror; the theme of belonging turned inside out.

chapters.title: Oscar's Lie
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Confrontation: Oscar confesses he is not a memory or a ghost but the House's first tenant, a child taken in 1931, reshaped into a lure. The ledger was never stolen to free the town—grandmother stole it to free Oscar, and failed. Beat: betrayal reframed as pity.

chapters.title: The Midpoint Bargain
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. At the threshold of the ledger room, the Archivist offers terms: return the ledger and the debt closes—but the account holder must remain to sign it. Jonah, exhausted and half-unmade, agrees. Beat: false resolution; the trap closes.

chapters.title: Above, While Jonah Was Below
chapters.summary: POV of Ruth and the town. The surface begins forgetting Jonah—photos blank, names slipping—while the tunnels' entrances seal one by one. Ruth, owing her own debt, chooses to break her silence and gather the owing families. Beat: the stakes widen beyond one protagonist.

chapters.title: The Ledger's True Page
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Reading the ledger before signing, Jonah finds the 1974 entry isn't a theft—it's a receipt. Grandmother didn't take the ledger; she took a page out of it, the page with Oscar's name, which is why the House has hunted her line. Beat: revelation that reframes the whole debt.

chapters.title: What the House Wants Back
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, racing. The House doesn't want the ledger returned; it wants the page, and the name on it restored—Oscar back inside the walls. Jonah realizes returning the ledger as bargained will re-imprison Oscar forever. Beat: moral crisis at the climax's edge.

chapters.title: Signing
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV. Climax. In the ledger room, Jonah signs—not returning the ledger but writing a new entry: their own name, offered as the Archivist's successor, in exchange for striking every debt in the book and releasing Oscar's page. The House resists; the room fills with every taken version of Jonah, and they choose which self to leave behind. Beat: sacrifice as authorship.

chapters.title: The New Archivist
chapters.summary: Second-person interlude, Jonah now the Archivist. They learn the work: recording, not collecting; keeping accounts honest. They amend the ledger, strike the town's debts, and feel Oscar's name leave the pages. Beat: eerie peace, power accepted and bounded.

chapters.title: Oscar, Unwritten
chapters.summary: Jonah's POV, from below. Oscar, freed of his tenant-shape, becomes an ordinary dead boy's echo—brief, grateful, gone. Jonah watches the door of the House close from the inside and understands they chose this belonging over the other kind. Beat: grief and love resolved.

chapters.title: The Porch Light, Revisited
chapters.summary: POV of Ruth, above. The tunnels are gone from every map and memory; the town wakes owing nothing and remembers almost nothing. Ruth alone keeps a drawing of a door and a name she can't place. On the old porch, the light burns steady. Beat: quiet aftermath.

chapters.title: Edmund Hartwell's Note
chapters.summary: Epilogue in the author's voice. Hartwell describes visiting Hollow Creek while surveying, finding a house with a lit porch and no owner of record, and a tin under the floorboards containing a ledger with one new entry: a thank-you, addressed to the reader. Beat: the horror hands itself to us; the debt, gently, continues.
